mcqs.question: A 4x4 matrix reduces to only 3 nonzero pivot rows after elimination. What does this tell you about the original 4 equations?
options: The system definitely has no solution
One of the four equations is redundant — a combination of the others, adding no new constraint
The system now has 4 independent unknowns to solve for
mcqs.explanation: Rank 3 out of 4 rows means only 3 of the equations are linearly independent — the 4th is expressible as a combination of the others and carries no new information. This alone doesn't determine solvability (that also depends on b); it specifically tells you about redundancy among the equations.

mcqs.question: After Gaussian elimination, one row reads 0 = 3 (all variable coefficients are zero, but the right-hand side is nonzero). What does this mean?
options: The system has infinitely many solutions
This row can simply be dropped and ignored
The system has no solution — the equations are contradictory
mcqs.explanation: A row reducing to 0 = c with c nonzero is a direct contradiction (no combination of variables can produce a nonzero constant from zero coefficients), meaning the system is inconsistent and has no solution. Dropping the row would silently hide that the original equations conflict.

mcqs.question: You feed slightly different (noisy) sensor data into the same exact linear solver twice, and get wildly different solutions each time. The matrix isn't singular. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The system is ill-conditioned — rows/columns are nearly collinear, so small input changes cause large output swings
The solver has a bug, since an exact solver should always be stable
The system has no solution at all
Ill-conditioning only affects overdetermined (least-squares) systems, not exact ones
mcqs.explanation: Ill-conditioning is exactly this symptom: a matrix that is technically invertible (nonzero determinant) but numerically close to singular, so tiny perturbations in input get massively amplified in the solution. It's a property of the matrix's geometry (near-collinear rows/columns), not a solver bug, and it applies to any solve, not just least squares.

mcqs.question: Your service needs to solve Ax=b for the same A against thousands of different b vectors arriving over time. Why would a production solver factor A into LU once, rather than computing A inverse once and reusing it?
options: Computing A inverse once and reusing it is actually the faster and more standard approach in production solvers
LU factorization and explicit inversion have identical numerical stability, so the choice makes no real difference
LU decomposition is generally more numerically stable and is the reusable factorization production solvers are built around, even though both approaches let you avoid refactoring A for every new b
LU decomposition must be redone for every new b, so it offers no reuse advantage over inversion
mcqs.explanation: Both explicit inversion and LU decomposition let you reuse a one-time O(n^3) factorization across many b vectors — the real reason production solvers default to LU is that it's generally more numerically stable, avoiding the extra rounding-error amplification that comes from forming and multiplying by an explicit inverse. LU factors (once computed) are reused via cheap O(n^2) forward/back substitution for each new b, not recomputed each time.
